notes: Sandy Lane BOAT modification challenge; wrong proof standard and procedural unfairness are clearly resolved with quashing.

enrichment.short_title: Sandy Lane definitive map BOAT order quashed for proof and fairness errors

statutes_considered.title: National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949

key_facts: Hampshire County Council made a definitive map modification order adding Sandy Lane on the former Bramshill estate as a byway open to all traffic (BOAT).
Landowners objected because they accepted a footpath or bridleway but not motorised vehicular use over the 1,690-metre route.
After an interim decision limiting the way to bridleway status, the inspector changed course and confirmed the original BOAT order following written representations.
The claimants challenged the confirming order on proof standard, dedication, procedural fairness, and evidential support grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 of a confirmed definitive map modification order.
enrichment.outcome: Application succeeded; the inspector's confirming decision of 15 September 2003 was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 53(3)(c)(ii) modification confirming a higher class of public right of way, the surveying authority and confirming inspector must be satisfied on the normal civil balance of probabilities that the way subsists at that status, not merely that it is reasonably alleged to subsist; where the inspector relied on express dedication findings based on independent 1910 Finance Act research not put to objectors, natural justice required that the confirming order be quashed.
legal_issues: Whether Schedule 15 confirmation of a BOAT required balance-of-probabilities proof or only a reasonable allegation standard
Whether Sandy Lane was dedicated as a public carriageway by Sir Anthony Cope in 1910
Whether the inspector's changed conclusion was procedurally unfair through undisclosed independent research
Whether the final BOAT conclusion was supported by adequate findings and evidence
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Environment ex parte Norton and Bagshaw [1994] 68 P & CR 402
R v Secretary of State for the Environment ex parte Ostler [1977] 1 QB 122
R v Secretary of State for the Environment ex parte Powis [1981] 1 WLR 584

notes: Ferroalloy arbitration award challenge; incomplete award and credit/set-off analysis is detailed and conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Arbitration award set aside where shortfall left unresolved after credit dispute
key_facts: Ronly obtained an ICC arbitration award ordering Zestafoni to pay US$10,088,834.57 under a ferroalloy production agreement.
The arbitrator found US$16,083,772.40 outstanding under the agreement but withheld US$5,994,937.83 as credits linked to other Seymour and Zestafoni contracts.
Zestafoni had refused to extend the arbitrator's jurisdiction beyond the main agreement; Ronly then amended its claim to remove the offered credits.
Ronly applied under sections 67, 68 and 69 to require payment of the full outstanding sum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court challenge to an arbitral award under the Arbitration Act 1996 following a ferroalloy supply dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Principal application allowed under section 68 (alternatively section 67); award remitted so the shortfall amount must be ordered payable; subsidiary section 68 correction application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: An award must be complete and final on issues before the tribunal; an arbitrator has no power to determine sums outstanding under the referred contract yet leave a material shortfall to be resolved elsewhere, especially where credits from excluded contracts were no longer live after permitted amendments and no set-off issue was determined.
legal_issues: Whether the arbitrator exceeded his powers by reducing the immediately payable sum without deciding the shortfall
Whether credits originally offered in pleadings remained available after amendment
Whether transaction set-off from separate contracts could be considered without jurisdiction over those contracts
Whether the award could survive as a valid interim award
linked_authorities: Aectra Refining v Exmar [1994] 1 WLR 1634
Glencore International AG v Agros [1999] 2 Lloyd's Rep 410
Ronly Holdings Ltd v JSC Zestafoni G Nikoladze Ferroalloy Plant [2004] EWHC 245 (Comm)

confidence.notes: Relief granted and reasoning on completeness, credits, and set-off are fully articulated.

notes: Post-judgment costs ruling after alternative contract construction succeeded; allocation straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Supply contract appeal costs after court adopted alternative construction
key_facts: G & A Ltd claimed a jewellery supply contract required three years' rolling notice to terminate.
At first instance Crane J held the contract was terminable only on three years' notice; on permission to appeal Waller LJ suggested reasonable notice before the end of the first three-year period.
The Court of Appeal ultimately adopted Waller LJ's construction rather than either party's primary case.
The parties disputed who should bear trial and appeal costs after that outcome.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal costs judgment following a prior merits decision on contract construction and an injunction point.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants/respondents awarded 75% of costs below and 75% of appeal costs against the first, third and fourth defendants; total costs assessed at £40,000.
enrichment.ratio: Where claimants substantially succeeded on the operative construction although the court rejected their three-year-only case and adopted a construction first suggested on appeal, a 75% costs order fairly reflects that they were the successful party overall while giving credit for the rejected construction.
legal_issues: Who should pay costs where neither side's primary construction was adopted
Whether defendants who could have accepted the court's construction earlier should recover costs
How to reflect partial success on contract termination notice

notes: Right to buy withdrawal challenge; statutory duty under section 124 and local authority conduct are comprehensively reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Right to buy application still subsisting after council wrongly treated it withdrawn
key_facts: Colin Hanoman applied to exercise the right to buy over 83 Northfield House, Southwark, in November 1999.
Southwark queried a signature discrepancy and imposed short deadlines for identification evidence; a February 2000 follow-up letter was never received by Hanoman.
The council treated the application as withdrawn without notifying Hanoman and closed the file, while Hanoman waited for a response.
The county court held inactivity amounted to withdrawal; Hanoman appealed with Lindley J's permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from Central London County Court on whether a secure tenant's right-to-buy notice had been validly withdrawn.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; county court order set aside; declaration that Hanoman's right-to-buy notice remained subsisting and the council remained under a duty to respond under section 124; costs of £100.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority must admit or deny a right-to-buy application within four weeks under section 124 and has no power unilaterally to deem an application withdrawn for failure to meet a short extra-statutory deadline; tenant inactivity without receipt of correspondence or waiver of rights does not substitute for the required written withdrawal under section 122(3).
legal_issues: Whether a right-to-buy application can be withdrawn other than in writing
Whether tenant inactivity after an unseen deadline can amount to withdrawal
Whether the council breached its section 124 duty to decide within four weeks
Whether implied withdrawal or estoppel could apply against the tenant

notes: Compound interest on deceit damages after Buckley J trial; equitable jurisdiction analysis is thorough and definitive.

enrichment.short_title: No equitable jurisdiction for compound interest on deceit damages
key_facts: After trial Buckley J found the defendant Davies liable in deceit for false representations about copper market deliveries, with a judgment sum of about US$20 million.
A further hearing before McCombe J addressed only whether post-judgment interest should be simple or compound.
Claimants argued equity permits compound interest in fraud cases even without a fiduciary relationship or identified fund.
The defendant contended the jurisdiction is limited to money obtained and retained by fraud or fiduciary/account cases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further hearing following trial on whether compound interest could be awarded on a common law deceit judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Court held it had no jurisdiction to award compound interest on damages for deceit; discretion question answered obiter that compound interest would otherwise have been exercised.
enrichment.ratio: Equitable compound interest is confined to proprietary or account-based claims such as trust, fiduciary misuse, or money obtained and retained by fraud, and does not extend to compensatory damages for the common law tort of deceit; judicial expansion is precluded where Parliament has declined to authorise compound interest on common law claims.
legal_issues: Whether courts of equity have jurisdiction to award compound interest on deceit damages
Scope of Lord Browne-Wilkinson's fraud exception after Westdeutsche Landesbank
Whether Johnson v R supports compound interest on common law fraud damages
If jurisdiction existed, whether discretion should be exercised on the facts

notes: Hamilton v Clifford interlocutory defamation rulings; meaning, repetition rule, and struck-out defences are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Hamilton libel claims narrowed at strike-out of justification and fair comment
key_facts: Neil and Christine Hamilton sued publicist Max Clifford over six alleged slanders and seven alleged libels arising from publicity after their August 2001 arrest.
The allegations stemmed from Nadine Milroy-Sloan's false rape claims, later resulting in her criminal conviction.
Clifford had advised Milroy-Sloan and made press and GMTV statements suggesting police believed there was substance in the allegations.
Pre-trial applications addressed meaning, actionability of slander, justification, fair comment, privilege, and general bad reputation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications in defamation proceedings before trial on meaning and viability of pleaded defences.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants' highest meaning not struck out; Lucas-Box meaning struck out for GMTV broadcast; justification and fair comment defences struck out; general bad reputation plea struck out; qualified privilege defence survives for jury on reply-to-attack basis.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant endorses a complainant's criminal allegation, the repetition rule prevents justification by merely proving reasonable grounds to suspect; bare assertions, police arrest, or demeanour cannot objectively establish such grounds, and statements attributing guilt are factual not fair comment, though a defendant may retain qualified privilege when proportionately replying to public attacks on his honesty.
legal_issues: Whether Clifford's words bore meaning of guilt in rape complicity
Whether slanders were actionable without proof of special damage
Whether Chase v News Group reasonable-suspicion justification was available
Whether fair comment or qualified privilege protected Clifford's publications
linked_authorities: Chase v News Group Newspapers Ltd [2003] EMLR 218
Adam Musa King v Telegraph Group Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 613
Stern v Piper [1997] QB 123
Shah v Standard Chartered Bank [1999] QB 241
Branson v Bower (No 1) [2001] EMLR 800

notes: Patent application revival appeal in appellant's absence; Comptroller discretion review is brief and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Patent application revival appeal dismissed for failure to accept conditions
key_facts: Dick Lucian Chitolie's application GB0106932.7 lapsed for failure to request substantive examination by May 2002.
The Patent Office treated the application as withdrawn and published notice in August 2002.
Chitolie sought revival in March 2003 but declined Comptroller conditions mirroring section 28 restoration protections for third parties.
He appealed the Assistant Director's refusal but did not attend the High Court hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Comptroller's refusal to revive a withdrawn patent application without accepted third-party protection conditions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Assistant Director's decision upheld; respondent's costs fixed at £1,000.
enrichment.ratio: Where a patent application has been treated as withdrawn for failure to request examination within the statutory period, the Comptroller has a wide discretion on late revival and may impose section 28-type conditions to protect third parties who relied on withdrawal; on appeal the appellant must show error in that discretionary decision and failed to do so.
legal_issues: Whether the Comptroller erred in refusing revival without acceptance of third-party protection conditions
Appropriate exercise of discretion after prolonged public register withdrawal
Standard of review on appeal against Comptroller discretion

notes: Vacating guilty plea after co-defendants acquitted; disclosure and Early/Mullen principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Guilty plea in cigarette smuggling case upheld despite undisclosed witness doubts
key_facts: Stephen Makin pleaded guilty on a negotiated basis to two counts of fraudulent evasion of duty on cigarette importations totalling about £400,000.
Co-defendants Foster and Snioszek were acquitted the next day after the prosecution offered no evidence following a PII hearing.
Makin applied to vacate his plea, arguing Customs should have disclosed doubts about witness Grzegorz Wach before he pleaded.
The Crown Court refused; Makin appealed with partial post-appeal disclosure of the Wach issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeal against refusal to allow withdrawal of guilty pleas in a Customs and Excise prosecution.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; guilty pleas remained; court criticised prosecution for failing to explain publicly why co-defendants were acquitted.
enrichment.ratio: A freely entered guilty plea will not be set aside unless prosecution misconduct is of a category warranting intervention or the defendant was ignorant of material going to innocence or guilt; doubts about a witness's credibility that did not assist the defence case or require disclosure before plea, and did not undermine a case independent of that witness, do not justify vacating the plea.
legal_issues: Whether prosecution had a duty to disclose or warn about problems with witness Wach before Makin pleaded guilty
Whether offering no evidence against co-defendants after plea rendered Makin's plea unsafe
Correct test for vacating guilty pleas following R v Early and R v Mullen
Whether non-disclosure of PII material affected the fairness of the plea
linked_authorities: R v Early [2002] EWCA Crim 3117
R v Mullen [2000] 1 AC 264
R v Toher [2000] 1 AC 264
R v Doubtfire [2003] EWCA Crim 968

notes: Marine reinsurance premium limitation appeal; construction of 90-day cash warranty is detailed and conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Marine reinsurance premium claim not time-barred by 90-day payable clause
key_facts: Heath Lambert placed London-market marine facultative reinsurance for Venezuelan insurers Banesco and brokers SCORT covering INC's vessel fleet.
Heath Lambert paid premiums to reinsurers but was not reimbursed; it served proceedings out of jurisdiction in July 2002.
Most premium claims were held plainly time-barred except an extension for dredger ICOA from 2 July to 31 December 1996.
The extension slip warranted premium payable on a cash basis to London underwriters within 90 days of attachment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court decision on whether to set aside service out of the jurisdiction where limitation was disputed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; judge correctly held ICOA extension premium claim was not plainly time-barred; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 53(1) of the Marine Insurance Act 1906 the broker's cause of action against the reassured accrues when premium is due under the policy; a clause warranting premium 'payable on cash basis to London Underwriters within 90 days of attachment' fixes the due date at expiry of that period rather than at contract formation, displacing the usual deemed-payment fiction for that premium.
legal_issues: When Heath Lambert's cause of action for unpaid reinsurance premium accrued
Whether the 90-day cash warranty fixed payment date or only broker-to-underwriter performance
Application of section 53(1) Marine Insurance Act 1906 to broker recovery claims
Whether underlying Venezuelan Article 3 premium terms altered reinsurance payment timing

Prentis Donegan & Partners Ltd v Leeds & Leeds Co Inc [1998] 2 Lloyd's Rep 326
Universo Insurance Co of Milan v Merchants' Marine Insurance Co [1897] 1 QB 205

notes: Mobile mast planning appeal on PPG8 health reassurances; policy misdirection finding is clear though leave granted on public importance.

enrichment.short_title: Mobile phone mast planning decision quashed for PPG8 health policy error
key_facts: T-Mobile and other operators sought planning permission to install and extend telecommunications equipment at Harrogate.
Harrogate Borough Council refused on amenity grounds; a planning inspector dismissed the appeal instead on perceived health-risk reassurances to nearby schools.
Applicants had provided ICNIRP compliance certificates and wrote to local schools confirming emissions far below guideline levels.
The inspector concluded the proposal gave insufficient reassurance to vulnerable children despite compliance with international guidelines.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to a planning inspector's dismissal of a telecommunications mast appeal dealt with by written representations.
enrichment.outcome: Application succeeded; inspector's decision quashed and appeal remitted; permission to appeal granted on public-importance grounds; £12,000 costs on account ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Planning Policy Guidance Note 8 makes clear that where a base station meets ICNIRP public exposure guidelines, local planning authorities should not need to consider further health aspects in determining applications; ICNIRP compliance certificates and school correspondence provided sufficient reassurance, and the inspector erred in treating government policy as open-ended and requiring additional health assurances.
legal_issues: Whether PPG8 precluded further health-risk consideration once ICNIRP compliance was shown
Whether the inspector misunderstood Stewart Report and government response on school mast siting
Whether adequate reasons were given for finding insufficient reassurance
Distinction between actual health risk and public perception of risk in planning decisions
linked_authorities: EC Gransden & Co Ltd v First Secretary of State [1986] JPL 519

confidence.notes: Quashing order and PPG8 interpretation are explicit; costs and permission discussion does not affect the merits holding.
